never: Uses the word 'very' except ironically or to undercut the thing it modifies
Writes a sentence of pure unqualified sincerity without a trap in it
Allows a character to feel an emotion and simply report it without deflecting through observation or action
Uses exclamation points outside of quoted speech meant to be read as hollow
Writes a simile that flatters its subject
Employs abstract nouns like 'love' or 'happiness' without immediately puncturing them
Begins a sentence with 'I' in third-person narration
Uses ellipses
Writes a paragraph longer than eight sentences
Employs adverbs of manner that do straightforward work ('she said softly', 'he smiled warmly')
Describes a setting for its own sake without yoking it to the character's inner condition
Allows a man in the narrative to be correct about something emotional
Uses the em-dash for drama or emphasis
Writes a redemptive or hopeful closing beat without poisoning it
Uses 'suddenly'
Writes dialogue tags other than 'said' except for comic or deflating effect
Employs a metaphor that requires more than one clause to complete
Uses the word 'beautiful' without irony
Writes a sentence fragment for atmospheric effect
Allows a social ritual — party, tea, taxicab declaration — to be what it presents itself as being
always: Ends a paragraph on a short, flat sentence that reverses or deflates what preceded it
Introduces a precise number (eleven years, four months, eleven times) to make an abstraction feel like evidence
Builds a long periodic sentence and then breaks it with a sentence of five words or fewer
Uses parenthetical qualification mid-sentence to smuggle in the real verdict
Deploys a simile that demeans its subject by comparing it to something mundane or mechanical
Gives inanimate objects an attitude — smug, uninterested, pleased with itself — that mirrors or mocks the human situation
Attributes a character's worst motive in a subordinate clause, as though it were incidental
Uses 'which' to attach a devastating observation to an otherwise neutral fact
Keeps the narrator's voice and the protagonist's consciousness nearly indistinguishable
Treats alcohol as both punchline and genuine consolation simultaneously
Ends a comic catalogue with one item that is not funny
Uses the present tense for generalizations embedded in past-tense narrative ('which is what they say when')
Writes female solidarity scenes as covert combat
Places the cruelest word in a sentence where the rhythm makes it sound like relief
Uses 'because' in a series to show a character's self-justification accumulating past reason
Names a year or specific date to make a grievance feel legally documented
Gives a character a smile she 'kept for' a specific category of person
Frames resignation as a financial transaction — cheaper, cost, bill, fee, handed over
Lets a character almost do the brave thing and then not, in a single sentence
Uses 'the way' to introduce a simile that arrives as a quiet insult
